rubric.description: States that the forces act between molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the forces as acting between molecules.

rubric.why: States the nature of the forces.
rubric.description: Identifies them as forces of attraction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the forces are attractive.

modelAnswer: Intermolecular forces are forces of attraction between the molecules of a substance.

items.followUp: What is meant by the malleability of a metal?

rubric.why: Defines malleability by the property of forming sheets.
rubric.description: States that metals can be beaten or hammered into sheets.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition of malleability.

rubric.why: Defines ductility by the property of forming wires.
rubric.description: States that metals can be drawn into wires.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition of ductility.

modelAnswer: Malleability is the property of a metal by which it can be beaten into thin sheets.
Ductility is the property of a metal by which it can be drawn into wires.

items.followUp: What is the value of one standard atmosphere in pascals?

rubric.why: Describes standard atmospheric pressure in context.
rubric.description: Identifies it as the pressure exerted by the atmosphere at sea level.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct description.

rubric.why: Gives a recognised standard value or equivalent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct standard-pressure value.

modelAnswer: Standard atmospheric pressure is the pressure exerted by the atmosphere at sea level.
It is 1 atm, equal to 760 mm Hg or 101325 Pa.

items.followUp: Why do gases have much larger volumes than liquids for the same amount of substance?

rubric.why: Identifies the large separation between gas particles.
rubric.description: States that gas molecules are far apart or have large intermolecular spaces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the large spaces between gas molecules.

rubric.description: Explains that the large spaces give gases low mass per unit volume and hence low density.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the spacing to low density.

modelAnswer: Gas molecules are far apart, with large spaces between them.
Therefore, a gas has less mass per unit volume and a low density compared with a liquid.

rubric.why: Identifies the solution's capacity to dissolve more solute.
rubric.description: States that an unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that more solute can dissolve.

rubric.why: Includes the temperature condition for solubility.
rubric.description: Specifies that this is at a given temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including the temperature condition.

modelAnswer: An unsaturated solution is a solution that can dissolve more solute at a given temperature.

items.followUp: Explain a 10% m/v sugar solution and give an example of how to prepare 100 mL of it.

rubric.description: States that % m/v is the mass of solute in grams per 100 mL of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct meaning of % m/v.

rubric.why: Provides a valid numerical example of the concentration.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as 5 g of NaCl in enough solution to make 100 mL of solution (5% m/v).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example with the correct solute mass and final solution volume.

modelAnswer: A % m/v solution contains the stated number of grams of solute in 100 mL of solution.
For example, a 5% m/v NaCl solution contains 5 g of NaCl in enough solution to make 100 mL.

items.followUp: What is a colloid? Give one example.

rubric.description: Defines the Tyndall effect as the scattering of light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that light is scattered.

rubric.why: Identifies the particles responsible or the observable result.
rubric.description: States that colloidal particles scatter light, making the path of the beam visible.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the scattering to colloidal particles or the visible beam path.

modelAnswer: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by colloidal particles.
It makes the path of a light beam visible in a colloid.

items.followUp: What is an oxidizing agent? Give one example.

rubric.why: Describes the reducing agent's effect on another substance.
rubric.description: States that a reducing agent reduces another substance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing its reducing action.

rubric.why: Includes oxidation of the agent or a valid example.
rubric.description: States that the reducing agent is itself oxidized, or gives a valid example such as hydrogen reducing copper(II) oxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct oxidation statement or example.

modelAnswer: A reducing agent is a substance that reduces another substance and is itself oxidized.
For example, hydrogen reduces copper(II) oxide to copper: H₂ + CuO → Cu + H₂O.
